description: Hi! I’m youssif elsawy, a Computer Engineering student at the Arab Academy for Science, Technology & Maritime Transport (AAST). I have hands-on experience in Python, AI, machine learning, computer vision, and simulation, and I enjoy working on anything related to computer engineering, from algorithms to building complete systems.
summary: Analog Finder measures how closely places on Earth match specific Moon and Mars sites, so mission teams can pick analog test sites by data instead of habit. We measured 9 real targets from orbital data (LRO LOLA, Diviner and Lunar Prospector in LROC QuickMap; MGS MOLA in Google Colab), then measured 10 factors for 59 Earth sites and whole-world scans in Google Earth Engine. NASA EMIT minerals, ESA permafrost maps and Sentinel-2 images check the best candidates, and an interactive map lets anyone pick a target and see every Earth site re-rank, with the source of every number. Results: the closest matches to Jezero Crater are two plateaus never proposed for Jezero, Aksai Chin (Karakoram-Kunlun) and the limestone plateau east of Kharga, Egypt, tied at 75% and above Haughton Crater (68%); EMIT shows Kharga's carbonate is uniform, making it the practical first field site. For a permanent Moon base, Harrat Khaybar, Saudi Arabia, is the best lava-tube shelter analog (76%) and the eastern Karakoram the best south-pole terrain outside Antarctica. The method ranks 13 of 15 known analog pairs in the top quarter.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Analog sites for Moon and Mars missions are usually chosen because they are known and reachable, not because anyone measured how well they match a specific target. Analog Finder measures it. For 9 real targets (lunar south pole, Mare Imbrium, the Mare Tranquillitatis pit, Descartes highlands; Jezero, Gale, Arcadia Planitia, the Arsia Mons pits and Meridiani Planum) we measured each target's conditions from orbital data: slope, iron, hydrogen, temperature and rock cover on the Moon in LROC QuickMap, and slope on Mars from MOLA in Google Colab.

HOW IT WORKS

We measured 10 factors for 59 Earth sites in Google Earth Engine: cold, dryness, temperature swing, thin air (altitude), relief, rock type, vegetation, ground ice, and site features such as caves and impact craters. A weighted similarity gives each site a match score per target. World scans at 5 km and 250 m close-ups search the whole planet for new areas; NASA EMIT minerals, ESA permafrost maps and Sentinel-2 images check the best ones. The interactive map lets anyone pick a target, re-rank every site, adjust the weights, and see a radar chart and the source of every number, plus travel time and protected status.

RESULTS

- Jezero Crater: two plateaus never proposed for Jezero, Aksai Chin (Karakoram-Kunlun, a disputed border area) and the limestone plateau east of Kharga Oasis, Egypt, tied at 75%, both above the classic Haughton Crater (68%). EMIT shows Kharga's carbonate is uniform (99-100% of detections at 6 spots) while Aksai Chin's is patchy, and Kharga is 4 hours from a city: the practical first field site. Egypt's Western Desert was compared to Mars in NASA-funded studies by Farouk El-Baz (1979-82), but its carbonate plateaus were never proposed for Jezero.

- Permanent Moon base: Harrat Khaybar, Saudi Arabia, is #1 of 59 sites for a lava-tube shelter (76%), ahead of NASA's cave analogs Lava Beds and El Malpais; the eastern Karakoram is the best match to the lunar south pole outside Antarctica.

- Mars base ice (Arcadia): the Tibetan Plateau (74%) is the best match outside Antarctica.

- Gale and Meridiani: Chile's Atacama coast range is a new #1.

DOES IT WORK?

13 of 15 well-known analog pairs rank in the top quarter, and 2,000 random re-weightings test how stable each result is. Scores are relative, so sites within about one point are treated as ties.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Mission planners and field scientists can find and justify analog sites for a specific landing site or base, compare options on the same scale, and see what each site lets a team practise (ice drilling, carbonate sampling, lava-tube operations).

TOOLS

Google Earth Engine (JavaScript), Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pandas, matplotlib), LROC QuickMap, NASA AppEEARS, Google Colab, D3.js and TopoJSON for the map, GitHub Pages for hosting.

LIMITS AND NEXT STEPS

Scans run at 1-5 km, so caves come from catalogs; EMIT covers only latitudes below 54 degrees; crew factors (isolation, dust, regolith) are not scored yet; no field visit yet. Next: visit the Kharga plateau, add crew factors, global mineral and cave catalogs, and the Artemis III and Mars human landing sites.

Use of AI: code and text were written with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic); all measurements were run and checked by the team.
